title: Given the dimensions of a chain of matrices, find the minimum number of scalar multiplications needed to compute the product, choosing the best parenthesization.
shortTitle: Matrix Chain Multiplication: interval DP for minimum multiplications
keyPoints: Matrix multiplication is associative, so the result is the same regardless of grouping, but the cost differs enormously
dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1]*p[k]*p[j] for split point k in [i, j)
A single matrix needs no multiplication, so dp[i][i] = 0 is the base case
Fill the table by increasing chain length so shorter subchains are ready before longer ones
Time is O(n^3) and space is O(n^2), where n is the number of matrices
Storing the optimal split index at each cell allows reconstructing the actual parenthesization

s1_definition.oneliner: Split the chain at k; cost = left + right + p[i-1] * p[k] * p[j]; take the minimum.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Matrix chain multiplication** – finding the optimal way to parenthesise a chain of matrices to minimise scalar multiplications.
- **Interval DP** – a dynamic programming pattern where the state is a contiguous range and the transition tries every split point.
- **Dimension array** – array `p` where matrix i has dimensions `p[i-1]` by `p[i]`.
- **Recurrence** – `dp[i][j] = min over k in [i, j) of dp[i][k] + dp[k+1][j] + p[i-1]*p[k]*p[j]`.
- **Base case** – `dp[i][i] = 0` because a single matrix needs no multiplication.
- **Complexity** – O(n^3) time and O(n^2) space.
s1_definition.analogy: A risk engine at National Bank of India multiplies a chain of covariance and factor matrices for a portfolio risk calculation. The order of multiplication drastically changes the arithmetic cost even though the result is the same. The engine tries every split point to find the cheapest grouping.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Matrix Chain Multiplication is the archetypal interval dynamic programming problem. Matrix multiplication is associative, so the final product is the same no matter how you group the operations, but the arithmetic cost differs enormously depending on the parenthesisation. The DP table dp[i][j] stores the minimum cost to multiply the subchain from matrix i to matrix j.

For each subchain, we try every split point k. The cost of splitting at k is the cost of multiplying the left group plus the cost of multiplying the right group plus the cost of combining the two resulting matrices. We take the minimum over all split points. The base case is that a single matrix needs no multiplication, and we fill the table by increasing chain length so shorter subchains are ready before longer ones.

At the National Bank of India, the portfolio risk engine multiplied a chain of covariance and factor matrices where the grouping order changed the floating-point cost by orders of magnitude. The engine ran this cubic interval DP to find the optimal parenthesisation before executing the actual multiplications. Storing the best split index at each cell also allowed reconstructing the grouping for debugging and audit.

Remember one sentence: matrix chain multiplication tries every split point within a range and picks the cheapest, which is the core idea of interval dynamic programming.
